title: How Do Extended Benefits Affect Unemployment Duration? A Regression Discontinuity Approach
research_question: How does a large extension of the maximum potential duration of unemployment benefits affect the duration of unemployment spells among older workers, and how do these effects differ between men and women given gender-specific early retirement rules?
data_description: The analysis combines two Austrian administrative data sources: the Austrian Social Security Database (ASSD), which records individuals' age, employment, unemployment, and earnings histories since 1972 along with employer region and industry, and the Austrian Unemployment Register (AUR), which provides place of residence (community) and socio-economic characteristics. The data cover the universe of unemployment inflows over 1986-1995, with spells followed until end-1998. The unit of observation is an individual unemployment spell. Unemployment duration is measured in weeks registered at the unemployment office (with time-to-next-job as a robustness measure). Analysis focuses on non-steel-sector inflows aged 46-53 with continuous work histories (actual-to-potential experience ratio at least 0.7), in pre-program (1/1986-12/1987) and program (8/1989-7/1991) windows. A community-level travel-time distance measure to the border between eligible and ineligible regions is constructed.
institutional_context: In June 1988, Austria introduced the Regional Extended Benefits Program (REBP), which extended the potential duration of unemployment benefits from 30 weeks to 209 weeks for job seekers who simultaneously satisfied three sharp criteria at the start of an unemployment spell: being aged 50 or older, having lived for at least six months in one of 28 selected labor market districts (concentrated in steel-restructuring areas in eastern Austria), and meeting a 780-week prior-employment requirement over 25 years. The program ran until August 1993. Austrian early retirement rules add a gender asymmetry: women could access early retirement at age 54 (via special income support after benefit exhaustion) and 55, while men only at 59-60. This setup creates two sharp eligibility thresholds—age 50 and the geographic border between eligible and ineligible regions—with otherwise identical labor market institutions across regions.
ground_truth_notes: Potential manipulation of age at entry into unemployment and regional differences in industry structure could affect results.
